<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, you’re dealing with an iOS library (with both Objective-C and Swift variants) that manages keyboard events – in particular, preventing the keyboard from covering UITextField/UITextView elements in an app. The library is split into a “core” functionality and several feature-specific modules (like text view support, return key handling, toolbar management, etc.) and even includes several demo projects to show sample integrations. Here’s how you can design a detailed system architecture/diagram:

1. Identify the Project Type and Purpose:
   • This is not a full-stack application but rather a UI/UX helper library designed to manage keyboard interactions within iOS apps.
   • The README emphasizes “One Line of Code” integration, automatic handling, no subclassing, and lightweight configuration.
   • Notice how the project has been modularized into multiple “published” repositories (for example, IQKeyboardCore, IQTextView, IQKeyboardReturnManager, IQKeyboardToolbar, etc.). This splitting indicates an architectural decision to keep loosely coupled components that can be reused according to need.

2. Analyze the File Structure Highlights:
   • Top-level directories include demo projects (both Objective-C and Swift versions) which serve as integration examples.
   • The main source folders are found in the “IQKeyboardManager” and “IQKeyboardManagerSwift” directories, each containing further subdirectories grouping related functionality (for example, Categories, Constants, and various UI component files).
   • Notice the separate configuration (Podfile, Package.swift, Cartfile) and Continuous Integration files (.travis.yml, .swiftlint.yml) which indicate the necessary build and quality assurance steps.
   • There are multiple documentation and migration guide files that provide context about how the components were refactored or split over time. This also tells you that part of the architecture is aimed at easy future migration and extension.

3. Creating the System Design Diagram:
   a. Main Components:
      – IQKeyboardManager (Core Library): Represents the main functionality to manage keyboard appearance and text input fields.
      – IQKeyboardManagerSwift: The Swift version and new variant that depends on several modular libraries.
      – Modular Subcomponents: Include modules such as:
           • IQKeyboardCore – the underlying helper functions (not meant to be installed directly).
           • IQTextView – for UITextView/placeholder functionality.
           • IQKeyboardReturnManager (formerly IQReturnKeyHandler) – for managing “next/previous/done” actions.
           • IQTextInputViewNotification – for monitoring text field/view events.
           • IQKeyboardToolbar and IQKeyboardToolbarManager – for configuring the accessory toolbar that accompanies the keyboard.
           • IQKeyboardNotification – for handling keyboard appearance/disappearance events.
      – Demo Projects: These serve to demonstrate the integration and use-case flows, both for Objective-C and Swift. They illustrate how the client (iOS app) interacts with the library.
      – Integration/Build Files: Files like the Podfile, Cartfile, and Package.swift indicate the dependency management and build system.

   b. Relationships and Interactions:
      – Show a layer for iOS system events (the OS sending keyboard appear/disappear notifications).
      – Draw an arrow from these OS events to IQKeyboardNotification, which listens for and catches these changes.
      – IQKeyboardNotification, IQTextInputViewNotification, and IQKeyboardReturnManager plug into the core IQKeyboardManager. Use directional arrows to demonstrate that the core library subscribes to notifications and then invokes adjustments on active UITextField/UITextView.
      – From IQKeyboardManager, illustrate how the accessory toolbar is configured by IQKeyboardToolbar and coordinated by IQKeyboardToolbarManager. 
      – Show that each modular component (typically represented as separate boxes) has dependencies on IQKeyboardCore functionalities.
      – Represent demo projects as “client applications” that integrate the IQKeyboardManager (Objective-C or Swift) and that trigger the overall sequence.

   c. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
      – Modularity: The system is split into independent modules (each with its own GitHub repository), allowing customization and swapping of functionality.
      – Loose Coupling: The design abstracts each responsibility (notification handling, return key management, toolbar operations) into individual modules that are interdependent via clearly defined interfaces.
      – Separation of Concerns: The core library handles the central logic, while additional features (toolbar, text view, etc.) are separate, easing maintenance and migration.
      – Dependency Inversion: The demo projects and even the library itself depend upon system notifications and events rather than coupling to concrete keyboard events.

   d. Technologies, Frameworks, and Libraries:
      – iOS platform components (UITextField, UITextView, UIKeyboard notifications)
      – Build tools such as CocoaPods, Carthage, and Swift Package Manager.
      – CI/CD tools indicated by Travis CI and swiftlint for code quality.
      – Xcode projects and workspaces indicate integration in the Apple development ecosystem.

4. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • For an iOS library like IQKeyboardManager, emphasize a layered diagram:
         - The bottom layer: iOS OS events (keyboard notifications, UI events).
         - The middle layer: IQKeyboardManager and its various submodules (each module gets its own box with labels such as “Keyboard Notification Listener”, “Text Input View Handler”, “Return Key Manager”, “Toolbar Manager”).
         - The top layer: Integration examples (Demo projects) showing the final interaction with the iOS app.
   • Use clear labels and directional arrows to show data flow—from the operating system to the modular components and finally to the end-use in the demo/integrated application.
   • Consider using color coding or distinct shapes; for example, squares for core libraries, circles or rounded corners for external dependencies, and dashed lines to indicate optional modules.

5. Instructing the Principal Software Engineer to Include:
   – Clearly label each component: “IQKeyboardManager Core”, “IQKeyboardNotification”, “IQTextInputViewNotification”, “IQKeyboardReturnManager”, “IQKeyboardToolbarManager”, etc.
   – Draw directional arrows to show how:
         • Keyboard events from iOS travel through IQKeyboardNotification.
         • IQTextInputViewNotification tracks which text field is active.
         • IQKeyboardReturnManager processes navigation (return/next keys).
         • IQKeyboardToolbar and its Manager work to add dynamic toolbars.
   – Include a separate box to denote “Demo Projects” (Objective-C and Swift versions) which simulate usage and integration.
   – Highlight build/integration elements (Podfile, Package.swift, Cartfile) as auxiliary components that facilitate dependency management.

6. Additional Details:
   – Add a legend or color coding: for instance, assign one color for “Core/Framework components”, another for “Modular Extensions”, and a third for “Integration / Demo”.
   – If possible, include migration notes in the diagram (perhaps a side note) that explains deprecated components and their newer alternatives, as documented in the README.
   – Ensure every arrow, component, and box is annotated with concise notes on function or dependency, making the diagram a reference for quick understanding.

By following these instructions, you will have a very detailed and accurate system design diagram that captures every essential architectural element of IQKeyboardManager, precisely tailored to its modular design, dependency management, and integration into iOS applications.
</explanation>
